analyses.title: Temporal Information Extraction by Predicting Relative Time-lines
analyses.research_question: Can temporal information be extracted more efficiently and consistently by directly predicting relative event time-lines instead of first predicting pairwise temporal relations?
analyses.methodology: The authors represent each temporal entity by a predicted start point and duration, yielding a relative time-line whose start and end points imply temporal relations. They introduce two direct models, a context-independent S-TLM and a contextual BiRNN-based C-TLM, plus TL2RTL, an indirect method that converts predicted TLinks into a consistent time-line. Three losses translate TimeML interval annotations into point-algebra constraints and are used to train the models. Evaluation uses TempEval-3-derived and TimeBank-Dense-derived splits and reports precision, recall, and F-score over temporal relations recovered from the predicted time-lines.

key_findings.finding: Direct relative time-line prediction can avoid pairwise temporal-relation extraction while producing temporally consistent outputs with linear prediction complexity in the number of entities.
On the TE3 evaluation split, contextual C-TLM with the regular time-line loss achieved F=56.1, exceeding all reported TL2RTL variants, whose best F-score was 52.8.
On the smaller TimeBank-Dense-derived split, indirect TL2RTL performed better than C-TLM, with the best TL2RTL result reaching F=62.3 while the best C-TLM result was F=58.4.
The regular time-line loss was the most robust of the tested losses and was also cheaper and more directly interpretable than losses requiring scores for every relation type.

The contextual direct model appears better than TL2RTL at correctly positioning temporally related entities that are farther apart in the text, consistent with reduced dependence on locally pruned pairwise TLink extraction.

The single-time-line representation does not explicitly separate actual, negated, hypothetical, expected, and opinionated events, which the discussion identifies as potentially belonging on separate temporal axes.
The proposed models produce relative ordering and inclusion information but do not yet map event positions or durations to absolute calendar times or physical durations.

limitations: The models assume temporal entities have already been detected; entity-recognition errors are not evaluated end to end.
The output is a relative time-line and cannot yet be mapped directly to calendar dates or absolute durations.
All events are placed on one time-line, although factual, negated, hypothetical, expected, and opinionated events may require separate time axes.
The smaller TimeBank-Dense-derived training split appears insufficient for C-TLM to exploit contextual parameters fully.
Simultaneous relations are particularly difficult, partly because they often involve event coreference.
The paper does not directly benchmark wall-clock prediction speed between direct and indirect implementations because implementation differences would make such a comparison unfair.
Evaluation against conventional temporal-relation systems is indirect because complete time-lines and sparse pairwise TLink predictions have different output structures.
raw_claims: Temporal information extraction is commonly decomposed into entity detection, temporal-relation extraction, and time-line construction.
The proposed direct paradigm skips explicit temporal-relation extraction and predicts entity start points and durations from text.
S-TLM predicts each entity's placement without contextual sequence encoding.
C-TLM uses bidirectional recurrent networks to incorporate textual context when predicting starts and durations.
The proposed losses convert TimeML-style interval relations into constraints over interval endpoints.
TL2RTL optimizes entity positions so that a predicted set of temporal links is satisfied as closely as possible.
More than 96 percent of the extracted TLinks were satisfied by the optimized TL2RTL time-lines despite some inconsistent input graphs.
C-TLM with the regular loss reached an F-score of 56.1 on TE3, compared with 52.3 for the corresponding TL2RTL variant.
The authors attribute some of the higher scores on the TimeBank-Dense-derived split to its denser annotation and different class balance.
Simultaneous relations were the most frequently violated relation type in the error analysis.
Correct relations unique to C-TLM involved event pairs farther apart in the text on average than relations correctly handled by both approaches.
The current system represents temporal entities on one relative axis rather than explicitly modeling factuality or modality-specific axes.
Code for the proposed methods is stated to be available.

analyses.title: Weakening conflicting information for iterated revision and knowledge integration
analyses.research_question: Can conflicts in prioritized knowledge bases be resolved with less information loss by weakening conflicting formulas rather than deleting them, while retaining practical computational behavior and desirable revision semantics?
analyses.methodology: The paper develops Disjunctive Maxi-Adjustment (DMA) for stratified propositional knowledge bases, replacing conflicting formulas at a priority level by progressively larger disjunctions until consistency is restored. It develops several logically related implementations, including DMA, Whole-DMA, and Iterative-DMA, and proves connections between the method and lexicographical inference. The authors compare the approaches theoretically with Adjustment and Maxi-Adjustment and experimentally on eight inconsistent DIMACS knowledge bases. Experiments measure retained/generated clauses and computation time, while a complexity analysis examines compilation size and query costs.

key_findings.finding: DMA resolves inconsistency by weakening formulas involved in conflicts through disjunction rather than simply discarding all conflicting formulas at the affected priority level.
DMA can preserve strictly more information than Maxi-Adjustment because information lost by removal can survive in weaker disjunctive form.

DMA inference is shown to be equivalent to lexicographical inference, providing a compiled consistent base without explicitly enumerating the potentially exponential set of lexicographically preferred subbases.
key_findings.section: 6 DMA as a compilation of the lexicographical system

key_findings.finding: In the eight reported DIMACS examples, standard Adjustment retained no clauses from the inconsistent second stratum, while DMA retained or generated at least as much information as Maxi-Adjustment and substantially more on several instances.

Whole-DMA was dramatically faster than kernel-computing MA, DMA, and IDMA on the eight reported examples, taking about 0.1 seconds per instance while some kernel-based runs required hundreds of seconds.
The speed advantage of Whole-DMA comes with potentially large compiled representations and weaker syntactic traceability to the original formulas.
Whole-DMA may require exponentially more space than the original stratified knowledge base in the worst case because it can generate combinatorially many disjunctions.

limitations: The formal treatment assumes stratified propositional knowledge bases with explicit priority ranks; the paper does not address extraction of such propositions or priorities from natural-language communication.
The experimental study uses only eight randomly selected inconsistent DIMACS bases, each with 50 variables and 80 or 100 clauses.
In the reported benchmarks, conflicts happened in the second stratum and no additional conflicts appeared later, limiting the diversity of revision patterns tested.
Kernel computation makes MA, DMA, and IDMA costly on larger knowledge bases.
Whole-DMA can produce exponentially large knowledge bases in the worst case.
Whole-DMA may obscure provenance and justification because original formulas can disappear syntactically from the compiled base.

The paper's treatment of revision is logical and priority-based rather than explicitly temporal; applying it to changing workplace event states would require a separate representation of time, source identity, and revision events.
raw_claims: Conflict resolution is treated as constructing a consistent knowledge base from ranked propositional information and new information.
Adjustment stops retaining lower-ranked material once it reaches an inconsistent stratum.
Maxi-Adjustment handles conflicts rank by rank but deletes formulas participating in conflicts.
DMA instead weakens conflicting formulas by replacing them with disjunctions of increasing size.
The DMA construction can preserve consequences that Maxi-Adjustment loses.
The paper proves that DMA and lexicographical inference produce equivalent consequences.
This equivalence avoids explicitly enumerating all lexicographically preferred consistent subbases.
The experiments use eight inconsistent DIMACS aim-50-no instances that were divided into strata of twenty clauses.
Whole-DMA avoids explicit conflict-kernel computation and was much faster on the reported experiments.
Kernel-based approaches were slow on some test instances because identifying formulas involved in conflicts is expensive.
Whole-DMA generated many more clauses than the other approaches in the experimental second strata.
Iterative-DMA preserves a representation closer to the original knowledge base but pays a larger computational cost.
Whole-DMA can require exponential compilation space in the worst case.
The proposed strategies are intended for iterated belief revision and integration of information from multiple sources.

analyses.title: Improving Temporal Relation Extraction with a Globally Acquired Statistical Resource
analyses.research_question: Can large-scale corpus-derived prior knowledge about the temporal ordering of event types improve local and globally constrained temporal-relation extraction?
analyses.methodology: The authors build TemProb by extracting verb-frame events and temporal relations from more than one million New York Times articles spanning 1987–2007, using semantic role labeling, learned temporal classifiers, and greedy transitive-closure inference. The resulting counts define prior distributions over temporal relations between pairs of semantic verb frames. They validate these priors against TimeBank-Dense and an EventCausality dataset, then inject the priors as features into local averaged-perceptron classifiers and as regularization terms in an ILP global inference model. Performance is evaluated using precision, recall, F1, temporal-awareness F-score, significance tests, and additional bootstrap stability analysis.

key_findings.finding: TemProb contains approximately 51,000 distinct verb semantic frames, 9.2 million verb-pair-relation entries, and up to about 80 million extracted temporal relations from the NYT corpus.
TemProb's before/after probabilities behave as meaningful confidence estimates on TimeBank-Dense: increasing the probability threshold raises precision while reducing recall.
On the converted EventCausality evaluation, using TemProb priors achieved 66.2% accuracy, an 11.5-point improvement over the majority T-Before baseline.

Adding the full TemProb prior distribution as local classifier features improved F1 by 2.7 points for same-sentence relations and 6.5 points for adjacent-sentence relations relative to the original local features.

Combining TemProb features and ILP regularization increased global TimeBank-Dense F1 from 46.2 to 52.1 and temporal-awareness F-score from 42.5 to 49.6, with the reported comparison significant at p<0.0005.
On the paper's partial TimeBank-Dense evaluation restricted to SRL-extracted verb events, the proposed system achieved F1=55.5 and temporal-awareness F=52.8, exceeding the two compared prior systems.
The resource is restricted to verb semantic-frame events and therefore does not directly cover nominal events or all events in complete TimeBank-Dense.
The automatically induced resource contains erroneous or context-sensitive event-pair statistics, particularly because event arguments and richer context are not represented in the pairwise priors.

limitations: TemProb is derived from New York Times news, so its event-order priors may be domain-specific and may not transfer directly to workplace email, chat, or operational logs.
Only verb semantic frames are modeled; nominal and other event types are omitted.
The event-pair statistics ignore arguments, which can make apparently anomalous temporal associations difficult to distinguish from extraction errors or special contexts.
TemProb is automatically generated using an imperfect temporal-relation extraction system, so extraction errors are propagated into the resource.
The training annotations and generated relations primarily cover same-sentence or adjacent-sentence event pairs, limiting direct modeling of longer-range relations.
The main comparison focuses on a partial TimeBank-Dense subset that matches SRL-extracted verb events rather than the complete benchmark.
The global regularization weight was heuristically fixed at 0.5 rather than selected through a reported systematic optimization.
Evaluation of EventCausality as temporal data assumes that causes temporally precede their effects.
The resource models typical temporal order, not event factuality, cancellation, revision, source authority, or contradiction states.
raw_claims: Temporal-relation decisions often require knowledge about the order in which event types usually occur.
TemProb was induced automatically from more than one million New York Times documents covering roughly twenty years.
Events are represented as disambiguated verb semantic frames extracted with semantic role labeling.
The temporal label set contains before, after, includes, included, equal, and vague.
Two temporal classifiers are trained separately for same-sentence and neighboring-sentence event pairs.
Greedy graph inference applies transitive closure whenever a new temporal relation is added.
The induced resource contains around 51,000 unique verb frames and roughly 80 million extracted relations.
Some verb pairs have highly stable tendencies to occur in one temporal order across the corpus.
Higher TemProb before-or-after confidence thresholds yield higher precision on TimeBank-Dense at the cost of recall.
The TemProb prior improved accuracy over a majority-label baseline on the EventCausality-derived temporal task.
Prior-distribution features produced larger gains for adjacent-sentence pairs than for same-sentence pairs.
Adding TemProb priors to both local classification and global ILP inference improved F1 and temporal-awareness scores.
The global model enforces uniqueness, symmetry, and transitivity constraints while rewarding agreement with TemProb.
TemProb does not cover all TimeBank-Dense events because it is restricted to events identified through verb SRL.
The authors made both the reported system and the TemProb resource publicly available.
